notes.front: What is Title VII?
notes.back: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which bars employment discrimination because of race, colour, religion, sex or national origin.
notes.explanation: Section 703 of the 1964 Act, codified at 42 U.S.C. 2000e-2, lists the unlawful employment practices.
notes.example: Like a rule that a hiring manager may weigh skills, but never a candidate's religion.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 2000e-2 (Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title VII, section 703), §2000e-2(a)(1)
notes.evidence: because of such individual's race, color, religion, sex, or national origin

notes.front: What is the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), title I?
notes.back: The federal law barring covered employers from discriminating against a qualified individual on the basis of disability in any aspect of employment.
notes.explanation: Its protection runs from job application procedures through hiring, pay, training and discharge.
notes.example: Like Title VII, but protecting people with disabilities and limiting medical questions.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 12112 (Americans with Disabilities Act, title I), §12112(a)
notes.evidence: No covered entity shall discriminate against a qualified individual on the basis of disability in regard to job application procedures

notes.front: What is the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA)?
notes.back: The 2008 federal law that, among other things, bars employers from discriminating because of genetic information and from acquiring it.
notes.explanation: Its employment title makes it unlawful to fire, refuse to hire or otherwise discriminate because of an employee's genetic information.
notes.example: Like the ADA, but about your genes and your family's medical history.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), short title note
notes.evidence: may be cited as the 'Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008'.

notes.front: What is the Employee Polygraph Protection Act (EPPA)?
notes.back: The 1988 federal law that generally bars private employers from requiring, requesting or using lie detector tests on employees or applicants.
notes.explanation: The prohibitions in section 2002 are subject to the exemptions in sections 2006 and 2007.
notes.example: Like a ban on a boss asking you to sit a lie-detector before your first shift.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. chapter 22 (Employee Polygraph Protection Act), short title note
notes.evidence: may be cited as the 'Employee Polygraph Protection Act of 1988'.

notes.front: What is an automated employment decision tool (AEDT)?
notes.back: A tool that automates or assists hiring and promotion decisions; New York City regulates employers' use of them under Local Law 144 of 2021.
notes.explanation: The city bars using such a tool unless it has been audited for bias within a year, the results are public and notices are given.
notes.example: Like a résumé-screening program that ranks applicants before any person reads them.
notes.source: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, Automated Employment Decision Tools, overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB)?
notes.back: The federal agency that administers the National Labor Relations Act, including employees' section 7 rights to organise and act together.
notes.explanation: Section 7 protects self-organisation, collective bargaining and other concerted activities for mutual aid or protection; the Board itself is established by 29 U.S.C. 153.
notes.example: Like a referee for disputes between employers and workers acting together.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. 157 (National Labor Relations Act, section 7), §157
notes.evidence: Employees shall have the right to self-organization, to form, join, or assist labor organizations, to bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing

notes.front: What is the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC)?
notes.back: The federal commission created under Title VII that enforces federal employment discrimination law, including GINA.
notes.explanation: GINA defines "Commission" as the EEOC created by 42 U.S.C. 2000e-4 and gives it the same powers it has under Title VII.
notes.example: Like a regulator you complain to when you think a hiring decision was discriminatory.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), §2000ff(1)
notes.evidence: "Commission" means the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission as created by section 2000e–4 of this title.

notes.front: What is the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)?
notes.back: The Department of Labor agency for workplace safety and health, acting under the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970.
notes.explanation: GINA refers to genetic monitoring rules the Secretary of Labor may issue under that 1970 Act; OSHA's own rules sit in Title 29, chapter 17, of the federal regulations.
notes.example: Like a building inspector, but for workplace hazards.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), §2000ff–1(b)(5)
notes.evidence: regulations that may be promulgated by the Secretary of Labor pursuant to the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970

notes.front: Besides refusing to hire or firing, what else does Title VII forbid employers to do because of a protected trait?
notes.back: Limit, segregate or classify employees or applicants in ways that deprive them of opportunities or harm their status.
notes.explanation: The same list of traits applies: race, colour, religion, sex and national origin.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 2000e-2 (Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title VII, section 703), §2000e-2(a)(2)
notes.evidence: to limit, segregate, or classify his employees or applicants for employment in any way which would deprive or tend to deprive any individual of employment opportunities

notes.front: When is a practice with a disparate impact unlawful under Title VII?
notes.back: When it causes a disparate impact on a protected basis and the employer fails to show it is job related and consistent with business necessity.
notes.explanation: The complaining party must first show the particular practice causes the disparate impact.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 2000e-2 (Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title VII, section 703), §2000e-2(k)(1)(A)(i)
notes.evidence: the respondent fails to demonstrate that the challenged practice is job related for the position in question and consistent with business necessity

notes.front: What does Title VII say about adjusting employment test scores by race or sex?
notes.back: It is an unlawful employment practice to adjust scores, use different cut-offs or alter results on the basis of a protected trait.
notes.explanation: The rule applies when selecting or referring applicants or candidates for employment or promotion.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 2000e-2 (Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title VII, section 703), §2000e-2(l)
notes.evidence: to adjust the scores of, use different cutoff scores for, or otherwise alter the results of, employment related tests on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin

notes.front: Before a job offer, what may an ADA-covered employer not ask an applicant?
notes.back: Whether the applicant has a disability, or the nature or severity of a disability; nor may it require a medical examination.
notes.explanation: The ban on disability questions and examinations applies to job applicants before any offer.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 12112 (Americans with Disabilities Act, title I), §12112(d)(2)(A)
notes.evidence: a covered entity shall not conduct a medical examination or make inquiries of a job applicant as to whether such applicant is an individual with a disability or as to the nature or severity of such disability

notes.front: What may an ADA-covered employer ask applicants before an offer?
notes.back: About their ability to perform job-related functions.
notes.explanation: Asking about ability differs from asking whether a person has a disability, which is barred before an offer.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 12112 (Americans with Disabilities Act, title I), §12112(d)(2)(B)
notes.evidence: A covered entity may make preemployment inquiries into the ability of an applicant to perform job-related functions.

notes.front: When may an employer require a medical examination under the ADA employment entrance rule?
notes.back: After a job offer and before work starts, if all entering employees take it regardless of disability.
notes.explanation: The offer may be conditioned on the results, which must be kept confidential and used only as the subchapter allows.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 12112 (Americans with Disabilities Act, title I), §12112(d)(3)
notes.evidence: A covered entity may require a medical examination after an offer of employment has been made to a job applicant and prior to the commencement of the employment duties of such applicant

notes.front: How must medical information from an ADA entrance examination be kept?
notes.back: On separate forms, in separate medical files, treated as a confidential medical record.
notes.explanation: Limited sharing is allowed, for example with supervisors about necessary work restrictions and accommodations.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 12112 (Americans with Disabilities Act, title I), §12112(d)(3)(B)
notes.evidence: is collected and maintained on separate forms and in separate medical files and is treated as a confidential medical record

notes.front: Under the ADA, who may be told about an employee's medical information from an entrance exam, and about what?
notes.back: Supervisors and managers, about necessary work restrictions and accommodations; first aid and safety staff, when emergency treatment might be needed.
notes.explanation: Government officials investigating compliance must also be given relevant information on request.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 12112 (Americans with Disabilities Act, title I), §12112(d)(3)(B)(i)-(ii)
notes.evidence: supervisors and managers may be informed regarding necessary restrictions on the work or duties of the employee and necessary accommodations

notes.front: When may an employer require a medical examination of a current employee under the ADA?
notes.back: Only when it is shown to be job-related and consistent with business necessity.
notes.explanation: The same test applies to questions about whether the employee has a disability or how severe it is.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 12112 (Americans with Disabilities Act, title I), §12112(d)(4)(A)
notes.evidence: unless such examination or inquiry is shown to be job-related and consistent with business necessity

notes.front: Which medical examinations of employees does the ADA expressly allow as part of a workplace health programme?
notes.back: Voluntary medical examinations, including voluntary medical histories, in an employee health programme available at that work site.
notes.explanation: Information obtained is subject to the same confidentiality rules as entrance examinations.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 12112 (Americans with Disabilities Act, title I), §12112(d)(4)(B)
notes.evidence: A covered entity may conduct voluntary medical examinations, including voluntary medical histories, which are part of an employee health program available to employees at that work site.

notes.front: Under GINA, what is genetic information?
notes.back: Information about a person's genetic tests, the genetic tests of family members, and diseases or disorders manifested in family members.
notes.explanation: It also includes requests for or receipt of genetic services, but excludes information about sex or age.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), §2000ff(4)(A)
notes.evidence: information about— (i) such individual's genetic tests, (ii) the genetic tests of family members of such individual, and (iii) the manifestation of a disease or disorder in family members of such individual

notes.front: What does GINA forbid an employer to do with genetic information, apart from discriminating?
notes.back: Request, require or purchase genetic information about an employee or an employee's family member, subject to exceptions.
notes.explanation: Acquisition is itself unlawful, so an employer cannot collect first and promise not to use it later.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), §2000ff–1(b)
notes.evidence: It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to request, require, or purchase genetic information with respect to an employee or a family member of the employee

notes.front: Which GINA acquisition exception covers an employer that asks about family medical history by accident?
notes.back: The exception for inadvertently requesting or requiring family medical history.
notes.explanation: Other exceptions cover wellness programmes, family and medical leave certifications and publicly available documents.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), §2000ff–1(b)(1)
notes.evidence: where an employer inadvertently requests or requires family medical history of the employee or family member of the employee

notes.front: On what employee authorisation may an employer-offered wellness programme collect genetic information under GINA?
notes.back: Prior, knowing, voluntary and written authorisation by the employee.
notes.explanation: Only the employee and the professional providing the services see identifiable results; the employer sees aggregates.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), §2000ff–1(b)(2)(B)
notes.evidence: the employee provides prior, knowing, voluntary, and written authorization

notes.front: Which purchased documents fall outside GINA's "commercially and publicly available" exception?
notes.back: Medical databases and court records.
notes.explanation: Newspapers, magazines, periodicals and books that mention family medical history are within the exception.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), §2000ff–1(b)(4)
notes.evidence: including newspapers, magazines, periodicals, and books, but not including medical databases or court records

notes.front: For what purpose may an employer conduct genetic monitoring under GINA, and with what notice?
notes.back: To monitor the biological effects of toxic substances in the workplace, with written notice to the employee.
notes.explanation: The employee must also authorise it in writing unless the law requires it, and be told the individual results.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), §2000ff–1(b)(5)
notes.evidence: to be used for genetic monitoring of the biological effects of toxic substances in the workplace, but only if— (A) the employer provides written notice of the genetic monitoring to the employee

notes.front: How must an employer keep genetic information it holds about an employee?
notes.back: On separate forms and in separate medical files, treated as a confidential medical record.
notes.explanation: Keeping it with ADA confidential medical records counts as compliance.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), §2000ff–5(a)
notes.evidence: such information shall be maintained on separate forms and in separate medical files and be treated as a confidential medical record of the employee or member

notes.front: Which body enforces GINA employment rules for employees covered by Title VII?
notes.back: The EEOC, with the same powers, procedures and remedies it has under Title VII.
notes.explanation: The Attorney General and private persons likewise have their Title VII powers and remedies.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), §2000ff–6(a)(1)
notes.evidence: shall be the powers, procedures, and remedies this chapter provides to the Commission, the Attorney General, or any person

notes.front: What are two things the EPPA forbids a covered private employer to do?
notes.back: Among others: require or request a lie detector test, and use or ask about any test results.
notes.explanation: It also forbids punishing an employee or applicant for refusing a test or because of the results.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. chapter 22 (Employee Polygraph Protection Act), §2002
notes.evidence: directly or indirectly, to require, request, suggest, or cause any employee or prospective employee to take or submit to any lie detector test; (2) to use, accept, refer to, or inquire concerning the results of any lie detector test

notes.front: Which devices does the EPPA count as lie detectors?
notes.back: Among others: a polygraph, a voice stress analyser and a psychological stress evaluator, used to give an opinion on honesty.
notes.explanation: The list ends with "any other similar device", so it is open.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. chapter 22 (Employee Polygraph Protection Act), §2001(3)
notes.evidence: "lie detector" includes a polygraph, deceptograph, voice stress analyzer, psychological stress evaluator, or any other similar device

notes.front: Does the EPPA apply to government employers?
notes.back: No. It does not apply to the U.S. Government, any state or local government, or their subdivisions.
notes.explanation: Separate national defence and security exemptions cover certain federal contractors.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. chapter 22 (Employee Polygraph Protection Act), §2006(a)
notes.evidence: This chapter shall not apply with respect to the United States Government, any State or local government, or any political subdivision of a State or local government.

notes.front: When may a private employer ask an employee to take a polygraph during an internal investigation, under the EPPA?
notes.back: In an ongoing investigation of economic loss or injury, where the employee had access and there is reasonable suspicion of involvement.
notes.explanation: The employer must also give the employee a signed statement about the incident before the test.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. chapter 22 (Employee Polygraph Protection Act), §2006(d)
notes.evidence: the test is administered in connection with an ongoing investigation involving economic loss or injury to the employer's business, such as theft, embezzlement, misappropriation

notes.front: Which private employers may polygraph prospective employees under the EPPA security services exemption?
notes.back: Firms whose primary business is providing armoured car personnel, security alarm staff or other security personnel protecting listed facilities or valuables.
notes.explanation: The protected functions include power, water and toxic-waste facilities and currency or precious commodities.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. chapter 22 (Employee Polygraph Protection Act), §2006(e)(1)
notes.evidence: by any private employer whose primary business purpose consists of providing armored car personnel

notes.front: Which employers does the EPPA drug security exemption cover?
notes.back: Employers authorised to manufacture, distribute or dispense scheduled controlled substances.
notes.explanation: Applicants must be headed for direct access to the drugs; current employees may be tested only in a related investigation.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. chapter 22 (Employee Polygraph Protection Act), §2006(f)(1)
notes.evidence: by any employer authorized to manufacture, distribute, or dispense a controlled substance listed in schedule I, II, III, or IV

notes.front: What notice must every employer covered by the EPPA display?
notes.back: A notice of the Act's pertinent provisions prepared by the Secretary of Labor, posted conspicuously where employee notices are usually posted.
notes.explanation: The Secretary prepares and distributes the notice; the employer posts and maintains it.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. chapter 22 (Employee Polygraph Protection Act), §2003
notes.evidence: Each employer shall post and maintain such notice in conspicuous places on its premises where notices to employees and applicants to employment are customarily posted.

notes.front: What civil penalty does the text of 29 U.S.C. 2005 set for an EPPA violation?
notes.back: Not more than $10,000.
notes.explanation: The Secretary weighs the employer's compliance record and the gravity of the violation when setting the amount.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. chapter 22 (Employee Polygraph Protection Act), §2005(a)(1)
notes.evidence: any employer who violates any provision of this chapter may be assessed a civil penalty of not more than $10,000

notes.front: Before procuring a consumer report for employment, what disclosure does the Fair Credit Reporting Act require?
notes.back: A clear and conspicuous written disclosure, in a document consisting solely of it, that a report may be obtained.
notes.explanation: The disclosure must come before the report is procured, and the consumer must authorise it in writing.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), §1681b(b)(2)(A)(i)
notes.evidence: in a document that consists solely of the disclosure, that a consumer report may be obtained for employment purposes

notes.front: Where may the consumer's written authorisation for an employment background report appear under the Fair Credit Reporting Act?
notes.back: On the same stand-alone disclosure document.
notes.explanation: The authorisation must be in writing, and the statute allows it to sit on the disclosure itself.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), §1681b(b)(2)(A)(ii)
notes.evidence: the consumer has authorized in writing (which authorization may be made on the document referred to in clause (i))

notes.front: Before taking adverse action based on a consumer report in employment, what must the employer give the person?
notes.back: A copy of the report and a written description of the person's rights under the Fair Credit Reporting Act.
notes.explanation: Both must be provided before the adverse action is taken, even if the report is only part of the reason.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), §1681b(b)(3)(A)
notes.evidence: before taking any adverse action based in whole or in part on the report, the person intending to take such adverse action shall provide to the consumer to whom the report relates— (i) a copy of the report

notes.front: Under New York City's Local Law 144, how recent must the bias audit of an automated employment decision tool be?
notes.back: Within one year of the tool's use.
notes.explanation: The employer must also make information about the audit public.
notes.source: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, Automated Employment Decision Tools, Local Law 144 of 2021 summary
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How far ahead of using an AEDT must New York City employers give candidates notice, according to the city agency?
notes.back: 10 business days before use.
notes.explanation: The city revised its roundtable slides in June 2023 to make that timing clear.
notes.source: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, Automated Employment Decision Tools, educational roundtables note
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which city agency enforces New York City's rules on automated employment decision tools, and since when?
notes.back: The Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, since 5 July 2023.
notes.explanation: People can complain to it when an employer skipped the audit, the published summary or the notices.
notes.source: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, Automated Employment Decision Tools, enforcement note
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What employee activity does section 7 of the National Labor Relations Act protect beyond joining unions and bargaining?
notes.back: Other concerted activities for the purpose of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection.
notes.explanation: Section 7 equally protects the right to refrain from such activities, subject to lawful union-security agreements.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. 157 (National Labor Relations Act, section 7), §157
notes.evidence: to engage in other concerted activities for the purpose of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection

notes.front: Which telephone equipment falls outside the Wiretap Act's "device" definition, so its use is not interception?
notes.back: Equipment furnished by the service provider and used by the subscriber in the ordinary course of its business.
notes.explanation: The exclusion turns on both how the equipment is supplied and that it is used in the ordinary course of business.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 119 (Wiretap Act, ECPA title I), §2510(5)(a)(i)
notes.evidence: furnished to the subscriber or user by a provider of wire or electronic communication service in the ordinary course of its business and being used by the subscriber or user in the ordinary course of its business

notes.front: How can prior consent make an employer's interception of employee calls lawful under the Wiretap Act?
notes.back: Where one party to the communication, such as the employee, has given prior consent, unless the purpose is criminal or tortious.
notes.explanation: The consent exception needs only one party, so a single consenting participant is enough.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 119 (Wiretap Act, ECPA title I), §2511(2)(d)
notes.evidence: where one of the parties to the communication has given prior consent to such interception

notes.front: A recruiter proposes lowering the pass mark on an aptitude test for applicants of one national origin. How does Title VII treat this?
notes.back: C: an unlawful employment practice.
notes.choices:
A) Lawful if it improves diversity
B) Lawful if applied to promotions only
C) An unlawful employment practice
D) Lawful if the test is voluntary
notes.choicesExplained: A: Title VII bars different cut-off scores on a protected basis whatever the aim. B: the ban covers promotion as well as hiring. D: voluntariness is not an exception.
notes.explanation: Using different cut-off scores on the basis of national origin is expressly unlawful.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 2000e-2 (Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title VII, section 703), §2000e-2(l)
notes.evidence: use different cutoff scores for, or otherwise alter the results of, employment related tests

notes.front: An automated screening tool rejects far more women than men for a warehouse job. The employer cannot show the screen is job related. Under Title VII, what is the risk?
notes.back: A: liability for disparate impact on the basis of sex.
notes.choices:
A) Liability for disparate impact on the basis of sex
B) None, because the tool is automated
C) None, because no one intended to discriminate
D) Only a notice duty under the ADA
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: disparate impact liability does not depend on who decides or on intent. D: the ADA concerns disability, not sex.
notes.explanation: A practice causing a disparate impact is unlawful where the employer fails to show it is job related and consistent with business necessity.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 2000e-2 (Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title VII, section 703), §2000e-2(k)(1)(A)(i)
notes.evidence: a complaining party demonstrates that a respondent uses a particular employment practice that causes a disparate impact on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin

notes.front: In a first interview, a manager asks a candidate, "Do you have any disabilities we should know about?" How does the ADA treat this question?
notes.back: D: prohibited before a job offer.
notes.choices:
A) Allowed if asked of every candidate
B) Allowed if the answer is kept confidential
C) Allowed, because it is only a question
D) Prohibited before a job offer
notes.choicesExplained: A: asking everyone does not make a pre-offer disability inquiry lawful. B: confidentiality applies to lawful post-offer exams, not to this question. C: inquiries are expressly covered.
notes.explanation: Before an offer, an employer may ask about ability to perform job functions but not whether the applicant has a disability.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 12112 (Americans with Disabilities Act, title I), §12112(d)(2)(A)
notes.evidence: make inquiries of a job applicant as to whether such applicant is an individual with a disability

notes.front: A firm makes conditional offers and then requires medical examinations only of applicants who mentioned past back surgery. Is this lawful under the ADA?
notes.back: B: no, entrance exams must apply to all entering employees regardless of disability.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, post-offer exams are always allowed
B) No, entrance exams must apply to all entering employees regardless of disability
C) Yes, if the results are kept in separate files
D) No, medical exams are never allowed
notes.choicesExplained: A: post-offer exams are allowed only on the statute's conditions. C: separate files are required but do not cure selective testing. D: exams after an offer are allowed if applied to all.
notes.explanation: The entrance examination exception requires that all entering employees be examined regardless of disability.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 12112 (Americans with Disabilities Act, title I), §12112(d)(3)(A)
notes.evidence: all entering employees are subjected to such an examination regardless of disability

notes.front: The personnel team keeps each new hire's entrance medical results in the ordinary personnel file that line managers can browse. What is wrong under the ADA?
notes.back: C: the results must be kept in separate medical files as confidential records.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, if the employee consented to the exam
B) Only that managers must sign a confidentiality pledge
C) The results must be kept in separate medical files as confidential records
D) The results must be destroyed after hiring
notes.choicesExplained: A: consent to the exam does not change how results are stored. B: a pledge does not satisfy the separate-file rule. D: the rule is confidential storage, not destruction.
notes.explanation: Entrance exam information must be kept on separate forms and in separate medical files as a confidential medical record.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. 12112 (Americans with Disabilities Act, title I), §12112(d)(3)(B)
notes.evidence: collected and maintained on separate forms and in separate medical files and is treated as a confidential medical record

notes.front: A new-hire onboarding form asks employees to list any heart disease in their parents. What does GINA say?
notes.back: A: requesting family medical history is generally an unlawful acquisition of genetic information.
notes.choices:
A) Requesting family medical history is generally an unlawful acquisition of genetic information
B) It is lawful because it is about parents, not the employee
C) It is lawful if kept confidential
D) GINA covers only the employee's own genetic test results
notes.choicesExplained: B: disease in family members is genetic information of the employee. C: acquisition is itself unlawful, apart from confidentiality. D: the definition also covers family medical history.
notes.explanation: Genetic information includes the manifestation of disease in family members, and employers may not request it except under listed exceptions.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), §2000ff(4)(A)
notes.evidence: the manifestation of a disease or disorder in family members of such individual

notes.front: A manager reads in a local newspaper obituary that an employee's mother died of a hereditary illness. Has the employer unlawfully acquired genetic information?
notes.back: D: no, newspapers fall within the commercially and publicly available documents exception.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, any knowledge of family history is unlawful
B) Yes, unless the employee consented
C) No, because obituaries are court records
D) No, newspapers fall within the commercially and publicly available documents exception
notes.choicesExplained: A: GINA lists exceptions, including public documents. B: consent is not needed for this exception. C: obituaries are not court records, and court records are excluded from the exception anyway.
notes.explanation: Buying commercially and publicly available documents such as newspapers is an exception, though medical databases and court records are not.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), §2000ff–1(b)(4)
notes.evidence: where an employer purchases documents that are commercially and publicly available (including newspapers, magazines, periodicals, and books

notes.front: A clothing retailer wants every job applicant to take a polygraph "to screen out dishonest people". What does the EPPA say?
notes.back: B: this is prohibited; no exemption covers routine screening by a retailer.
notes.choices:
A) Allowed if applicants consent
B) Prohibited; no exemption covers routine screening by a retailer
C) Allowed for part-time roles only
D) Allowed if the results are kept confidential
notes.choicesExplained: A: consent is not an exemption; even requesting a test is unlawful. C: the Act draws no part-time distinction. D: using results at all is barred.
notes.explanation: Private employers may not require, request or suggest lie detector tests except within the listed exemptions.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. chapter 22 (Employee Polygraph Protection Act), §2002(1)
notes.evidence: to require, request, suggest, or cause any employee or prospective employee to take or submit to any lie detector test

notes.front: After cash vanishes from a safe, a jeweller asks the two employees who had the combination to take polygraph tests, giving each a signed statement of the incident. Which EPPA provision is most relevant?
notes.back: C: the limited exemption for ongoing investigations of economic loss.
notes.choices:
A) The exemption for government employers
B) The drug security exemption
C) The limited exemption for ongoing investigations of economic loss
D) The national defence exemption
notes.choicesExplained: A: the jeweller is a private employer. B: no controlled substances are involved. D: that exemption concerns federal counter-intelligence testing.
notes.explanation: The ongoing investigation exemption covers theft where the employee had access and the employer has reasonable suspicion and gives a signed statement.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. chapter 22 (Employee Polygraph Protection Act), §2006(d)
notes.evidence: the employee had access to the property that is the subject of the investigation

notes.front: A state police department requires polygraph tests of recruits. How does the EPPA apply?
notes.back: A: it does not apply to state or local government employers.
notes.choices:
A) It does not apply to state or local government employers
B) It bans the tests outright
C) It allows them only with a court order
D) It applies unless the state opts out
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the Act simply excludes state and local governments. D: the exclusion is automatic, not an opt-out.
notes.explanation: The EPPA does not apply to the U.S. Government, state or local governments, or their subdivisions.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. chapter 22 (Employee Polygraph Protection Act), §2006(a)
notes.evidence: This chapter shall not apply with respect to the United States Government, any State or local government

notes.front: An employer puts its background-check disclosure in paragraph 14 of a long job application with a liability waiver. What is the Fair Credit Reporting Act problem?
notes.back: D: the disclosure must be in a document consisting solely of the disclosure.
notes.choices:
A) None, if the applicant signs the form
B) The disclosure must be given only after the report is obtained
C) The disclosure must be spoken, not written
D) The disclosure must be in a document consisting solely of the disclosure
notes.choicesExplained: A: a signature does not cure a disclosure buried in other terms. B: it must come before the report is procured. C: it must be in writing.
notes.explanation: The Fair Credit Reporting Act requires a clear and conspicuous written disclosure in a stand-alone document before procuring the report.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), §1681b(b)(2)(A)(i)
notes.evidence: a clear and conspicuous disclosure has been made in writing to the consumer at any time before the report is procured or caused to be procured, in a document that consists solely of the disclosure

notes.front: An employer reads a background report showing an old conviction and wants to withdraw the offer immediately. What must it do first under the Fair Credit Reporting Act?
notes.back: B: give the applicant a copy of the report and a written summary of rights.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, if the report is accurate
B) Give the applicant a copy of the report and a written summary of rights
C) Obtain a second report from another agency
D) Ask the applicant's written consent to withdraw the offer
notes.choicesExplained: A: the pre-adverse action duty applies whether or not the report is accurate. C: the statute does not require a second report. D: no consent to the decision is required.
notes.explanation: Before adverse action based in whole or part on the report, the employer must provide a copy and a description of rights.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), §1681b(b)(3)(A)
notes.evidence: (i) a copy of the report; and (ii) a description in writing of the rights of the consumer under this subchapter

notes.front: A New York City employer starts using a résumé-ranking tool without any bias audit. Under Local Law 144, what follows?
notes.back: C: it may not use the tool until an audit within the past year is done and published.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, if a human makes the final decision
B) It must merely notify candidates afterwards
C) It may not use the tool until an audit within the past year is done and published
D) The tool is lawful if bought from a vendor
notes.choicesExplained: A: the law turns on use of the tool, not on who signs off. B: notice is required, but so are the audit and publication. D: buying from a vendor does not remove the employer's duties.
notes.explanation: The law prohibits using such a tool unless it had an audit for bias within one year of use and the audit information is public.
notes.source: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, Automated Employment Decision Tools, Local Law 144 of 2021 summary
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Several employees post together on social media about unsafe staffing and low pay, urging colleagues to push for change. Which law most directly protects this activity?
notes.back: A: section 7 of the National Labor Relations Act, as concerted activity for mutual aid or protection.
notes.choices:
A) Section 7 of the National Labor Relations Act, as concerted activity for mutual aid or protection
B) The EPPA
C) GINA
D) The Stored Communications Act
notes.choicesExplained: B: the EPPA concerns lie detectors. C: GINA concerns genetic information. D: the SCA concerns stored communications, not the right to act together.
notes.explanation: Section 7 protects employees engaging in concerted activities for collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. 157 (National Labor Relations Act, section 7), §157
notes.evidence: other concerted activities for the purpose of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection

notes.front: A call centre records customer service calls after each agent signs a consent form. Under the federal Wiretap Act consent exception, is the recording lawful?
notes.back: D: yes, because a party to each call has given prior consent.
notes.choices:
A) No, every customer must also consent
B) No, employers may never record calls
C) Yes, but only calls on personal phones
D) Yes, because a party to each call has given prior consent
notes.choicesExplained: A: federal law needs only one party's consent. B: the consent exception is available to employers. C: personal phones are not the test; consent is.
notes.explanation: Interception is lawful where one of the parties has given prior consent and the purpose is not criminal or tortious.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 119 (Wiretap Act, ECPA title I), §2511(2)(d)
notes.evidence: where one of the parties to the communication has given prior consent to such interception

notes.front: An employee believes she was passed over for promotion after her employer learned of her genetic test result. With which agency would she typically file under GINA?
notes.back: B: the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.
notes.choices:
A) The National Labor Relations Board
B) The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
C) The Occupational Safety and Health Administration
D) The Federal Communications Commission
notes.choicesExplained: A: the NLRB deals with concerted activity and labour relations. C: OSHA deals with workplace safety. D: the FCC regulates communications.
notes.explanation: GINA gives the Commission, defined as the EEOC, its Title VII powers and procedures for GINA violations.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), §2000ff–6(a)(1)
notes.evidence: provided in sections 705, 706, 707, 709, 710, and 711 of the Civil Rights Act of 1964

notes.front: How do the ADA and GINA differ in what they let an employer collect, given that both require separate confidential files?
notes.back: The ADA allows post-offer medical exams of all entrants; GINA generally forbids even requesting genetic information.
notes.explanation: GINA treats genetic information kept as an ADA confidential medical record as meeting its own storage rule.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21F (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act), §2000ff–5(a)
notes.evidence: maintained with and treated as a confidential medical record under section 12112(d)(3)(B) of this title

notes.front: How do the EPPA and the ADA differ in what they allow before employment starts?
notes.back: The EPPA bars most private employers from polygraphing applicants; the ADA allows medical exams after an offer if all entrants take them.
notes.explanation: The EPPA's bar reaches requesting a test at all, subject to narrow exemptions.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. chapter 22 (Employee Polygraph Protection Act), §2002(1)
notes.evidence: to require, request, suggest, or cause any employee or prospective employee to take or submit to any lie detector test
